title: Q&A: How does AI affect our engagement at work?
excerpt: AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement.
content_html:
AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement.

What have you found?

We've found that new technology does not automatically lead to higher productivity or increased engagement at work. At the same time, technology changes job tasks, the distribution of responsibilities, skill requirements and opportunities to have a say in one's own work, while also increasing the intensity of work as simple, less demanding tasks disappear. That's why the same technology can lead to both increased engagement and frustration.

A key finding is that work engagement is not determined by the technology itself, but by how the technology affects the ability to perform work that is perceived as meaningful, manageable and conducive to development. We therefore focused on understanding the interplay between people, technology and work organization when new technology is introduced.

We are currently developing a framework to help researchers, employers, labor unions and systems developers identify factors that strengthen or could weaken work engagement in digitalized work environments.

What types of working environments have you investigated?

We have studied organizations in the IT sector, agriculture and rail transport. These are interesting because they are all undergoing rapid technological development, with AI, automation and robotization playing an increasingly significant role. This enables us to identify which effects appear to be sector-specific and which are more general for working life in the future.

Did you see any common patterns, and if so, what were they?

Yes, more than we initially expected. One clear pattern is that technology is no longer merely a tool. It plays an active role in how work is organized, prioritized and carried out. Employees work with technology, not alongside it.

We also found that people across different sectors describe meaningful work in surprisingly similar ways. It involves being able to use one's skills, make professional judgments, solve problems and contribute something of value. Technology can enhance this by eliminating routine tasks, but it can also undermine it if the parts of the work that create meaning are automated away.

What is needed for technology to boost work engagement?

The most important thing is that technology is designed to support people, not to replace the aspects of the job that foster motivation and professional pride.

Our findings suggest that work engagement is strengthened when technology frees up time for skilled tasks, increases opportunities to use one's skills and gives employees a say in how the work is carried out.

Who's behind this story?
